articles.summary: Is London City's Daniëlle van de Donk the unsung hero of the WSL season so far?
articles.body:
Radio 5 Live , · 19 Oct 2026 , · 48 mins

Ellen White and Ben Haines are back and Ellen starts by telling us about an exciting new job role. Joined by Em Sanders, the team react to Sarina Wiegman’s two-year contract extension with England and unveil the inaugural ‘Golden Goggles’ award for the best celebration of the week! There’s a WSL debrief focusing on the standout performances of Lauren James, Daniëlle van de Donk, and Océane Hurtré so far this season. Plus, we look at the big talking points ahead of this weekend’s derby games in North London and Manchester. articles.title: Transfobia contra Erika Hilton: Câmara de Ouro Fino abre processo | G1
articles.standfirst: Denúncia envolve comentário publicado em rede social pela vereadora Vânia Aparecida Vieira Couto sobre a deputada federal Erika Hilton; parlamentar tem 10 dias para apresentar defesa.
articles.summary: A Câmara de Ouro Fino apura denúncia de transfobia da vereadora Vânia Couto contra Erika Hilton; a parlamentar tem 10 dias para apresentar sua defesa.
articles.body:
A Câmara Municipal de Ouro Fino (MG) aprovou a abertura de uma comissão processante para apurar uma denúncia de transfobia contra a vereadora Vânia Aparecida Vieira Couto, do Podemos. A formação da comissão foi votada durante a sessão ordinária realizada no dia 13, após os vereadores receberem uma denúncia protocolada em 8 de outubro.

De acordo com a denúncia, a vereadora teria publicado um comentário em uma rede social sobre a deputada federal Erika Hilton. No conteúdo, ela teria questionado o gênero da parlamentar, utilizado o pronome masculino para se referir à deputada e feito outras manifestações consideradas transfóbicas.

Após o recebimento da denúncia, os vereadores votaram favoravelmente à abertura da comissão processante. Durante a sessão em que o tema foi discutido, Vânia Aparecida Vieira Couto utilizou uma fita na boca em sinal de protesto.

Câmara de Ouro Fino apura denúncia de transfobia por comentário de vereadora sobre deputada Erika Hilton — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

Segundo a Câmara Municipal, a vereadora já foi notificada sobre o processo e tem o prazo de 10 dias para apresentar sua defesa.

Encerrado esse período, a comissão processante deverá analisar os argumentos apresentados. O grupo terá mais cinco dias para avaliação e tomada de decisão.

A reportagem da EPTV entrou em contato com a vereadora. Ela agradeceu o espaço, mas informou que não irá se manifestar neste momento.

articles.title: Papa fala ao telefone com Zelensky | G1
articles.standfirst: Na última sexta (16), o pontífice teve uma ligação com o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, também para tratar da situação da cidade de Oleshky.
articles.summary: Na última sexta (16), o pontífice teve uma ligação com o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, também para tratar da situação da cidade de Oleshky.
articles.body:
Papa Leão XIV conduz oração no Vaticano após ter alta do hospital — Foto: Yara Nardi/Reuters

O papa Leão XIV conversou ao telefone nesta segunda-feira (19) com o presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelensky, segundo o Vaticano . Durante a ligação, o pontífice pediu cooperação entre a Ucrânia e a Rússia para permitir a entrada de ajuda humanitária e alimentos na cidade ucraniana de Oleshky, que está sob controle russo.

➡️ Ocupada pela Rússia, a cidade ucraniana de Oleshky enfrenta uma grave crise humanitária . Segundo a Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU), a cidade está sem estoque de alimentos nem combustível .

Na última sexta-feira (16), quando ainda estava hospitalizado, o pontífice havia conversado ao telefone com o presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin.

Segundo o Vaticano, na ocasião Leão XIV pediu que Putin pausasse os ataques para permitir a entrada de suprimentos e a saída voluntária de moradores de regiões da Ucrânia atualmente sob fogo cruzado.

Leão XIV expressou ainda "grave preocupação" com a situação humanitária em Oleshky a reiterou o "compromisso do Vaticano com o diálogo para a paz".

🔎 No início da guerra, o papa Francisco chegou a se oferecer para mediar o conflito e colocou o Vaticano como local de negociações, mas a proposta foi rejeitada pelo Kremlin.

O papa Leão XIV fez a ligação do hospital, onde estava internado após passar por cirurgia para a retirada de um tumor no pulmão. O pontífice teve alta no último sábado (17) .

Logo após a ligação, o governo russo afirmou que estava "construindo uma zona de segurança" dentro da Ucrânia - a qual incluiria Oleshky - e disse que não faria "parte de nenhuma negociação com Kiev".

O jornal "The Washington Post" afirmou que a última entrega de alimentos na cidade foi em maio.

articles.title: Gaza faces worsening hunger as WFP announces food aid cuts
articles.summary: The World Food Programme has announced that funding shortages will force it to suspend food assistance in Gaza
articles.body:
Gaza faces worsening hunger as WFP announces food aid cuts

The World Food Programme has announced that funding shortages will force it to suspend food assistance for half a million Palestinians in Gaza and reduce rations for others. Gaza’s Government Media Office has warned of “catastrophic consequences” and called for the reopening of border crossings to allow the delivery of urgent aid.

articles.title: Reuters/Ipsos: aprovação de Trump bate recorde negativo e chega a 31% | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento publicado nesta segunda-feira (19) mostra que 66% dos americanos reprovam o trabalho do presidente. Insatisfação com a economia também bateu recorde.
articles.summary: Levantamento publicado nesta segunda-feira (19) mostra que 66% dos americanos reprovam o trabalho do presidente. Insatisfação com a economia também bateu recorde.
articles.body:
A aprovação do presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , bateu um novo recorde negativo e chegou a 31%, segundo uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos divulgada nesta segunda-feira (19). A desaprovação também renovou a máxima histórica, atingindo 66%.

A pesquisa ouviu 1.679 adultos nos Estados Unidos entre 16 e 19 de outubro, pela internet. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos.

66% desaprovam o trabalho de Trump (eram 65% em 5 de outubro);

31% aprovam o trabalho de Trump (eram 32% em 5 de outubro);

Em todas as áreas avaliadas, a desaprovação supera a aprovação de Trump. Veja o saldo por tema:

A pesquisa apontou um aumento acentuado na insatisfação do eleitorado com a economia e o custo de vida no país. Ao todo, 68% desaprovam a forma como o presidente conduz as políticas econômicas.

O índice é seis pontos percentuais superior ao registrado em 5 de outubro e representa o pior resultado da série histórica dos dois mandatos de Trump.

A pesquisa também perguntou aos eleitores como pretendem votar nas eleições de meio de mandato, conhecidas como midterms , marcadas para 3 de novembro. No pleito, os americanos vão renovar todas as cadeiras da Câmara dos Deputados e cerca de um terço do Senado.

Entre os eleitores registrados para votar, 47% disseram que pretendem escolher um candidato do Partido Democrata, de oposição a Trump. Outros 35% afirmaram que vão votar no Partido Republicano, do presidente.

Segundo a agência, a vantagem de 12 pontos percentuais dos democratas é a maior registrada nas pesquisas Reuters/Ipsos sobre a eleição deste ano.

Atualmente, tanto a Câmara quanto o Senado são controlados pelo Partido Republicano. Os dados indicam que os democratas têm chances de conquistar a maioria nas duas Casas.

O agregador de pesquisas do site Race to the White House aponta que, atualmente, os democratas têm 73% de probabilidade de conquistar a maioria no Senado e 89% na Câmara.

articles.title: Tommy Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters, trial hears
articles.summary: The activist is accused of "bully-boy tactics" and denies harassment causing fear of violence.
articles.body:
Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.

Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.

The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."

Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.

Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case – and said his court fees to date had cost him £400,000.

Holt said that after the murders of three young girls in Southport on 29 July 2024, Yaxley-Lennon made a number of posts on social media. This alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.

The Daily Mail published articles that included photographs of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".

Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he made a series of posts on his X account in response.

On 4 August, these included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."

Another post said: "The daily mail have purposely doxed the exact location of my family. How can they be allowed to do this'."

There were no identifiable pictures of Yaxley-Lennon's children published by the Daily Mail or in the Mail Online, jurors were told.

Holt said the trial was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to the articles, and accused him of using "bully-boy tactics" to "intimidate" the journalists.

"He chose to frighten them, arrange for individuals to go to their addresses," said the prosecuting counsel.

"On social media — to millions of followers — he circulated images of their homes.

"His supporters got involved — threatening the journalists.

"Understandably, you might agree, they were scared; in some circumstances, being forced to leave their homes."

The court heard that on 5 August, Dirnhuber received a number of direct messages from Robinson/Yaxley-Lennon.

These included "you have endangered my children", "I'll be knocking at your door," and "let your bosses know I'm coming to all of your houses".

The jury panel also heard details of an alleged phone conversation between Yaxley-Lennon and Young.

"He said that he had Mr Young's telephone number. He recited his home address," Mr Holt told jurors.

Yaxley-Lennon then became, according to Mr Young, "increasingly menacing".

The prosecutor continued: "He raised his voice, he was swearing and shouting.

"He said that he had been researching Mr Young's family and threatened to publish photographs of them and their addresses online.

"Mr Lennon told Mr Young that he would be coming to Mr Young's house and he would have to move house.

"He was going to shove a camera in his face and ask questions.

"Mr Young told him that he did not want to engage with him — all complaints should be directed to the Daily Mail legal department.

"Mr Young believes Mr Lennon said 'I'm coming to get you'."

The prosecutor said it would have been "inevitable" that Robinson's posts would lead his supporters to "pick up the baton" and target the journalists. He referred to a post from somebody who had displayed a picture of Mr Young's Suffolk address online.

The prosecutor said: "This was never going to be a one-man campaign; it was inevitably going to draw others in."

Editor-in-chief of the newspaper Ted Verity also provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual identifying himself as "Tommy Robinson", who allegedly told him that he had "already located every... one of you".

The jury was told that Yaxley-Lennon's case was that his family "had been put in danger by the actions of the Daily Mail" and he had acted to "protect his family".

On X he posted: "What is good for the goose is good for the gander."

The trial, in front of a jury of nine men and three women, is expected to last for five days.

articles.title: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.summary: Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone.
articles.body: Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone. The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia. Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission. The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said. “At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added. The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video. The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit. The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.” In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.” The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties. The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment. Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries, commercial warehouses and data centers. “This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added. Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month. Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense. The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air. “During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”

articles.title: ‘Weight of responsibility’: Promise and perils of covering Ethiopia’s war
articles.summary: Al Jazeera correspondent shares his experience of covering the fighting between government forces and Tigray rebels.
articles.body:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – On September 23, fighting erupted in Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray, shattering the peace agreement between the Ethiopian government and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed nearly four years ago.

The latest fighting between the federal government-backed Tigray Peace Force (TPF) and TPLF started in the Erbeti area of Ethiopia’s Afar region after the 2022 peace deal unravelled over disarmament and territorial claims.

For me, the latest war is more than a story unfolding on television. It brought back painful memories of what I had experienced during my reporting in November 2021. The previous episode of fighting killed more than half a million people and displaced about 2 million others by the time the rival sides signed a deal to end the war in 2022.

After I was assigned to cover the fighting, I was once again faced with the challenge any war correspondent faces: how to stand in the midst of active fighting as a witness to the truth.

Soon, our team set off from the capital, Addis Ababa, to the Afar region and then to Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, covering the journey by road.

When I reached Erbeti, about 900km (560 miles) northeast of Addis Ababa, I hoped to catch my breath for a few hours and organise our coverage. Instead, events overtook us immediately.

Residents were leaving the town, which, until the previous day, had seemed safe. Small trucks and cars were piled with belongings. Men hurried to load whatever they could carry as families tried to get away before the fighting drew closer.

As we were still figuring out what to do next, loud sounds of shelling shook us. We decided to leave Erbeti only hours after arriving as staying would put the team’s lives at risk.

That had not been the plan. But war pays little attention to a correspondent’s plans.

We withdrew towards Afdera, about 100km (60 miles) to the east via unpaved roads. Afdera is a small town that serves as the administrative centre for the district of the same name in the Afar region, known for its salt mining.

We spent the night inside our car in the middle of the desert with the temperature hovering above 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit).

The next day, we started early to review information, make calls, prepare footage for reports and coordinate with the newsroom in Doha, Qatar.

Meanwhile, the heat and humidity drained our remaining energy as the mercury hit 50C (122F). As we lay in the car trying to catch some sleep, my thoughts were still in Erbeti.

Early the next morning, we headed for Afdera. After arriving there at 7am, we found that breakfast choices were limited.

The town followed a different rhythm: Many residents ate breakfast after dawn prayers, then headed to work. It was part of a correspondent’s daily reality – arriving somewhere unfamiliar and learning its routines.

We headed north towards Erbeti again, only to find the fighting intensifying in the mountains between the government-backed forces and TPLF.

I couldn’t see the clashes directly, but their sounds filled the area. The sound of artillery firing became louder as we got closer. At one point, we were barely 3km (almost 2 miles) from the front line.

We put on body armour and helmets, picked up our cameras and approached the government troops stationed on the front line.

We managed to film some footage and record brief accounts from soldiers. Then the assignment ended abruptly when the soldiers ordered us to evacuate immediately.

There was no time to argue or capture a final shot. We gathered our equipment and left with the shelling still echoing through the mountains behind us.

For days, we travelled difficult mountain routes through the regions of Afar, Amhara and Tigray. Roads we travelled on in the morning couldn’t be used by evening. Reports received before noon needed checking again before sunset.

In villages near the front lines, fear was visible in the faces we encountered as mothers packed small bags and children watched the road with anxious eyes.

I made a point of listening with sensitivity, respecting their suffering without exploiting their emotions for the camera.

As our coverage continued, the journey led us towards Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. We arrived the day after Ethiopian federal forces and their allies entered the city. The TPLF forces had retreated.

But Mekelle was a different city. I had expected it to be alive with unfolding events. It looked exhausted, with the usual police and security presence absent. It seemed to be trying to absorb what had happened in the hours before.

Daily life continued cautiously. Cars moved quietly through the streets, and shops had reopened in some neighbourhoods.

We saw soldiers welcomed in some streets while others remained silent, fearful of what might come next.

Many people declined to speak on camera because they didn’t know how events would unfold. There was no disorder in the conventional sense, but apprehension was everywhere. It was difficult to establish who was maintaining order or what the coming hours might bring.

We had no assurances about what might lie ahead. The possibility that our exit routes might close weighed on every decision.

Still, we had to keep working. Our audience was waiting for pictures and news. As far as we knew, we were the only media team in Mekelle.

I felt the weight of that responsibility. When you are alone in a place like this, every word matters. You must distinguish between what you have witnessed, what residents tell you and what the warring parties announce.

In a city that has only just emerged from battle, verifying information becomes harder than obtaining it.

We maintained as normal a routine as possible, filming in the morning, returning to prepare reports and following developments hour by hour.

The challenges extended beyond security. We also faced the demanding ethical task of preserving impartiality and professional distance in a deeply polarised war.

People in the Tigray region have historic grievances against the federal government. After coming to power in 2018, President Abiy Ahmed reformed political institutions, lifted media censorship and freed thousands of political prisoners. But ethnic tensions have since erupted in this diverse nation of 139 million people.

Documenting residents welcoming incoming government-backed troops without presenting those scenes as universal or reporting fears about withdrawing TPLF fighters without drawing definitive conclusions could expose us to accusations of bias from any party that wanted us to see the battlefield exclusively through its own eyes.

That’s why I went beyond what the camera captured, talking to residents and listening to those who preferred to speak off camera. I understood that our task involved listening not only to what people said but also to what remained unspoken.

Their accounts helped us understand the situation. With each hour in the city, we tried to weigh the different narratives, recognising that our observations and residents’ accounts offered distinct perspectives.

The exhaustion of days on the road had accumulated, but my mind stayed on the day just ended and the one ahead. Which road would we take? Where would we go? Would the events of the coming hours allow us to complete our plans?

After two weeks of moving between front lines, fatigue had become a constant companion.

While we kept reporting, rumours that we were arrested or trapped inside the city kept our colleagues and family members anxious. They searched for the smallest piece of information confirming we were safe.

Only after I appeared live on TV did I understand that it carried another meaning. For many who had been trying to reach us, it was more than a live report. It was an unintended reassurance that we were still there – and still alive.

I later learned that some Mekelle residents had discovered that government forces had taken control of their city from our broadcast.

With communications disrupted and information scarce, television was bringing people news of events unfolding close to their homes.

After three days of reporting, we left Mekelle, carrying testimonies and documented facts.

On the return journey, looking through the car window at the roads we had travelled over the previous two weeks, I reflected that memories of war are not confined to battlefields.

What remained were the faces of the people I had met along the way, the anxiety in people’s eyes and the persistent sense that life seeks to continue, even in the places closest to war.

articles.title: Dramatic images show violent unrest sweeping across France
articles.summary: France unrest protest photos over the weekend Macron election buildup
articles.body: Widespread violence erupted across France over the weekend, as rioters and looters ransacked storefronts, clashed with police and set fire to municipal buildings. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, the French Interior Ministry said, after some of the worst unrest the country has seen in years. In cities across the country, demonstrators set fire to newsstands and smashed windows. The violence followed weeks of largely peaceful protests over the cost of living and school conditions that expanded with an attempt to revive the “yellow vest” movement Saturday. In Limoges, a town in central France, dramatic scenes emerged overnight Saturday as rioters broke into the historic town hall and set it ablaze. Aerial images the following morning revealed the smoldering remains of the 19th century building, which had survived two world wars, capping one of the most violent days in France’s recent history. Across the country in Lyon, southeastern France, an elderly man wearing a gas mask fled from tear gas at the Place des Terreaux on Saturday. Crowds massed along the narrow streets of Paris throughout the weekend as masked demonstrators set up burning barricades near Place de la Republique, a major intersection through the city. Striking scenes of disorder emerged from the French capital, including the monument at Place de la Republique where masked demonstrators burned flares and waved flags on Saturday. Nearby, a man with a crucifix bearing the message “Love will triumph” rested near a burning vehicle in central Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for the violence. “Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he said.

articles.title: US-Ukraine relationship worsens amid Trump and Zelensky’s mutual distrust
articles.summary: The relationship between Ukraine and the United States is facing increasing strain over intelligence sharing, sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy and the path to peace.
articles.body: The relationship between Ukraine and the United States is facing increasing strain over intelligence sharing, sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy and the path to peace. There also appears to be deepening mutual distrust between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump on Monday accused Zelensky of not knowing what he was talking about and suggested it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.” Over the weekend Kyiv launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia, hitting a key oil terminal, in defiance of Trump’s demand that Ukraine stop hitting Russian refining plants. The White House is trying to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices in the US ahead of crucial midterm elections, as diesel prices are at a record high. Last week Trump called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and said Zelensky was more difficult to deal with than Russian leader Vladimir Putin. In an interview on Sunday, Zelensky hit back, saying it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face,” an apparent reference to Trump’s relationship to Russia. Trump again criticized Zelensky on Sunday, claiming in a Truth Social post that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” The relationship now seems to be at its lowest ebb since the explosive meeting at the White House 18 months ago. Zelensky has consistently said he is open to peace negotiations if Ukraine’s security can be guaranteed. The Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards the goal of peace. “We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X. “Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” Zelensky added on Monday. Zelensky also spoke to Pope Leo XIV on Monday, according to the Vatican. The pope spoke to the Ukrainian president just days after a phone call with Putin in which he expressed his concern about the “grave humanitarian situation” in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where Ukrainian authorities say around 2,000 civilians are stuck without access to food or basic medicine. Trump has defended recent concessions to Russia on sanctions, which have included a waiver to allow Russian diesel exports and another exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in his Sunday post. In an interview Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waivers strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield. There is growing anxiety in Kyiv and Europe that the Trump administration will make further concessions to Moscow in an effort to get Putin to agree to a peace deal. Zelensky told “Meet the Press” that the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” He said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin. Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.” On Monday, Zelensky appealed directly to the US Congress, holding an online meeting with a group of lawmakers from both parties. He described the current situation as “the most difficult situation from the very beginning of this war” and saying that it appears as if “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.” Ukraine is also perturbed by reports of a possible three-way meeting involving the US and China next month on settling the conflict – without Ukrainian involvement. “I think there’s been talk of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan Monday. Such a meeting would not help peace but “would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Monday. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” Sybiha wrote on X. The Kremlin said Monday that “no concrete proposals or agreements – neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content – have been discussed or put forward by anyone.” Attacks persist Defying Trump’s demands, Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. One target at the weekend was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike. A logistics center in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform. One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities. A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday. On Monday, Zelensky said a Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region killed six people, including three children. Sharing a blurred photograph of one of the victims – a small child in a stroller – Zelensky said the horrific image showed “the truth about this war.” “Lives must be protected. Ukraine needs air defense. You can’t think about making money with Russia as long as it continues its asinine war,” he said on X. Accusations have also flown over the cuts in US satellite intelligence provided to the Ukrainian military. Zelensky repeated on Sunday that changes in the Starlink system owned by billionaire Elon Musk was limiting the speed of its short-range and battlefield drones, describing it as a “message from the American government.” Musk said last week that the systems are owned and controlled by the US government, meaning that only the government could decide to place limits on their speed or usage. The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. On Monday, Trump said he didn’t know who it was that restricted it, but would “like to find out.” Similarly the Trump administration has pushed back on accusations from Kyiv that intelligence on incoming ballistic missiles is not being shared. Zelensky said on Monday that Kyiv had received no advance warning of ballistic missile attacks on Sunday night – something he claims has occurred multiple times in the past week. “Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners.” US satellite networks are critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. Russian ballistic missile attacks are aimed at crippling civilian life and destroying essential infrastructure. “I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio told ‌reporters Monday. “You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.” “What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused ​on,” Rubio said of Zelensky. Kyiv and Washington see very different paths to that goal. CNN’s Daria Tarasova, Anna Chernova, Julia Benbrook, Jennifer Hansler, Christopher Lamb, Kristen Holmes and Ivana Kottasová contributed to this report.

articles.title: Putin proposing summit with Trump, Xi in push to end Ukraine war: WSJ
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin is proposing a three-way meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss the war in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal Reported. Putin proposed the summit during a phone call with Trump on Oct. 9, the Journal reported, citing a Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter.…
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is proposing a three-way meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss the war in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal Reported .

Putin proposed the summit during a phone call with Trump on Oct. 9, the Journal reported, citing a Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. That phone call resulted in Trump announcing he would waive sanctions on Russia to buy diesel from the country, an effort to lower prices exacerbated by the U.S. war against Iran.

That move, alongside Trump waiving newly authorized sanctions on major importers of Russian energy, drew widespread condemnation from Kyiv and its allies in Congress. Reports of the White House ordering a slowdown in satellite services Ukraine relies on for air defense have further inflamed Kyiv’s allies in protesting Trump’s handling of the war.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Monday he believes there’s been “talks of a meeting,” when asked about The Wall Street Journal report. Rubio, who also serves as the president’s national security adviser, is on diplomatic travel to Uzbekistan.

“I think the president is open to anything that he can do to help bring the war to an end if it’s possible,” Rubio continued, adding that nothing’s been finalized.

The Journal reported Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed discussions about a potential trilateral meeting.

The White House and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Hill.

Such a summit, in particular excluding Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, is unacceptable to Kyiv, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote Monday on the social platform X.

The summit would only encourage Putin to continue the war, Sybiha wrote.

“Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve. He is not a global leader; he is a war criminal. And Russia is not a global power; it is a global problem,” Sybiha said.

A potential Putin-Trump-Xi summit could take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), scheduled to take place Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen in southern China.

The Journal reported that such a summit could serve to elevate Xi as a negotiator and signal the three leaders carving the world into spheres of influence. But Chinese officials are also weighing the downside of a high-profile trilateral summit overshadowing China hosting APEC and promoting Beijing’s role in the region.

articles.title: Top tourist destination in the world shuts down amid violent protests
articles.summary: Protesters in Paris barricaded the Louvre's iconic glass pyramid and entrances, forcing the world's most visited museum to shut down amid turmoil across the city.
articles.body: The Louvre, the globe's most visited and prominent museum, has closed its doors as turmoil sweeps across Paris. The institution, which houses renowned masterpieces like the "Mona Lisa," announced on Monday that it has shut down due to protesters barricading the entrances, pushing the disruption past a weekend of nationwide riots and demonstrations, according to local newspaper Le Monde. "Dear visitors, due to student strikes, the museum is currently closed. We apologize for the inconvenience," the Louvre wrote in a post on X. FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY No reopening time was provided at the time of publication. Visitors arriving for a Monday morning visit found the iconic glass pyramid, as well as the Carrousel du Louvre and Passage Richelieu entrances, barricaded by protesters from the École du Louvre, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP). The blockade — organized in solidarity with nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and recent police actions — forced management to turn away crowds at a site that normally draws up to 20,000 visitors on its busiest days, French media reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The disruption extends far beyond the Louvre's courtyards. Following a weekend of violent street clashes that left hundreds of businesses damaged and led to nearly 2,400 arrests across the country, other top Paris destinations, including the Eiffel Tower and major central shopping districts, have been heavily affected as international travelers navigate a city gripped by mass demonstrations and heightened security cordons, according to The Associated Press (AP). The Eiffel Tower was recently forced to turn away visitors and close its operations for a full day after staff initiated a sudden strike, AP reported. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The monument's unionized employees organized the walkout to protest limitations placed on female staff members during a private delegation's visit, completely halting public access to the world-famous iron structure, according to several French media outlets. Outside the immediate city center, the Château de Versailles has also faced abrupt closures that have derailed tourists' itineraries. The sprawling palace had to close its interior doors to the public on Oct. 6 following a severe power outage in the surrounding area, Xinhua News Agency reported. articles.title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.summary: The court upholds a decision to lift an arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont linked to the independence bid he led in 2017.
articles.body:
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.

The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.

Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.

But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.

Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.

In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.

It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.

The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.

Ex-Catalan leader ‘eludes police manhunt and flees Spain’

Catalonia's bid for independence from Spain explained

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests

Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.

He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.

Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.

While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.

Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.

In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.

"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.

It is still not known when he might return to Spain.

Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.

The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.

The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.

But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.

The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.

But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.

And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

articles.title: Pakistan suspends Iran border trade, amid violence on both sides
articles.summary: Islamabad cites security concerns, while Tehran points to technical issues as Pakistan mediates between Iran and the US.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan has halted trade with Iran at the Taftan and Gabd-Rimdan crossings in Balochistan province, leaving freight stranded on both sides of the border.

The suspension decision emerged on Saturday, as the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry (QCCI) in the provincial capital said about 2,000 trucks were stuck on both sides.

Passenger traffic at Gabd-Rimdan has continued, reported the Iranian news agency WANA.

Pakistan’s federal government has not commented publicly. Al Jazeera received no response from authorities in Balochistan, as both Islamabad and Tehran have offered different explanations for the border closure.

Bakhtiar Ismail, deputy commissioner of Chagai district, where the Taftan crossing is located, described the move as a security measure.

“Pakistan-Iran border closure is a temporary measure to improve border management to support counterterrorism efforts. The border will be opened as soon as effective measures are in place,” he wrote on X on Saturday.

Shahid Rind, an aide to Balochistan’s chief minister on political and media affairs, wrote on X the same day that the closure was meant to address security concerns, prevent smuggling and make the border system more effective.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, gave a different explanation.

“Due to certain technical issues and the necessity of implementing precautionary measures, cross-border movement and exchanges have been temporarily halted,” he said, according to the IRNA state news agency.

Imtiaz Baloch, a Quetta-based independent researcher who focuses on security in Balochistan, said security might be only part of the explanation.

“Although Pakistani officials have cited security concerns, the decision to close the border appears to be motivated by broader strategic considerations, with security as a possible factor amid economic sanctions on Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.

Javad Heiran-Nia, who heads the Persian Gulf Studies Group at the Center for Scientific Research and Middle East Strategic Studies in Iran, said Tehran’s wording could cover several issues.

“In my view, these expressions could refer to operational and administrative problems at border crossings, customs procedures, the verification of trade documents, financial transactions, or tighter security controls,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28. Islamabad brokered a ceasefire on April 8, but it collapsed within days. The US subsequently blockaded Iran’s southern ports.

With Iranian ports blocked, an April 25 Commerce Ministry order allowed third-country goods to be trucked to Iran along six routes ending at Gabd and Taftan.

In June, Pakistan and Qatar brokered the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed electronically by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

It called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, lifting the blockade and 60 days of talks on a lasting settlement.

The agreement lasted about a month. In July, Iran said it was no longer bound by parts of the deal after the US resumed attacks and its naval blockade.

Washington has since widened its sanctions. On August 24, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a campaign called Operation Economic Outcast, extending sanctions to shipping, gold, aviation and digital assets.

Earlier this month, Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistan would continue to comply with all applicable sanctions regimes, without specifying which.

Official bilateral trade between Iran and Pakistan is not massive – about $2.8bn in 2023-24, including $684m in Pakistani exports, according to the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI). Analysts say decades of US sanctions on Iran are a major factor.

But the US and the pressure it imposes on countries like Pakistan are not the only factors that influence Islamabad’s approach towards the border with Iran.

Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province, covers 44 percent of the country with a population of almost 15 million in the 2023 census.

The country’s poorest province, which borders Iran, has seen several uprisings since 1948. The latest, led by Baloch nationalist rebels, has continued for two decades.

The rebels accuse the state of exploiting local natural resources while communities remain deprived.

The number of attacks has risen sharply this year. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based think tank, recorded 62 security personnel killed in Balochistan in July, up from six in June. In September, it counted 225 attacks by armed groups nationwide, the highest monthly figure in 12 years.

At least 20 police personnel were abducted from a van in Mastung district on Friday.

Two days later, an army major was killed by an improvised explosive device in Gwadar district, said the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

Violence too in Chagai, the remote Balochistan district bordering Iran. Four travellers, including a customs official, were abducted from a coach there earlier this month.

Security analyst Imtiaz Baloch said Pakistani officials have long blamed the violence on porous borders.

“However, the issue goes beyond border permeability alone. Although armed groups remain active in the region, their mobilisation appears to be directed towards specific targets, and there is currently no clear indication of a broader mobilisation of armed groups on either side of the border,” he said.

Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, just across the border, has also seen repeated attacks on security forces.

On October 9, Nosrat Eftekhari, a senior official in the provincial police command, was killed by a roadside bomb near Zahedan, Iranian media reported. The killing followed several other security-related incidents.

Days later, on October 14, the commander of a women’s unit of the Basij paramilitary force was shot dead outside her home in Mehrestan district, Tasnim news agency reported. Another officer was killed in a separate attack on a police vehicle in the same district.

A coalition of Baloch armed groups formed last December, with Jaish al-Adl, a Sunni Baloch armed group established in 2012, as its main member, has claimed some of those attacks in Sistan-Baluchestan province.

Tehran has long accused the group of operating from Pakistan, but Islamabad has repeatedly said it has no organised presence on Pakistani soil.

Heiran-Nia cautioned against linking the attacks directly to Pakistan.

“It is important to distinguish between the presence of armed groups in Pakistan and evidence that they crossed the border to carry out a specific attack,” he said.

Tehran-based political analyst Seyed Reza Hashemi Jebeli said Tehran wanted the Pakistani government to do more to prevent cross-border attacks.

“The key issue for Tehran is that Pakistan should meet its commitments to prevent anti-Iranian armed groups from operating in border areas,” he told Al Jazeera.

Tehran’s accusations are not new. After Jaish al-Adl claimed an attack in December 2023 that killed 11 Iranian police officers, Iran’s then foreign minister urged Pakistan to take action.

On January 16, 2024, Iran carried out missile and drone attacks in Panjgur, another border district. Pakistan said the attacks killed two children. Two days later, Pakistan struck targets in Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, killing at least nine people. Intense diplomacy calmed tensions on the border and the neighbours agreed to expand security cooperation.

Heiran-Nia said a prolonged closure of the border crossings could test Pakistan’s role as mediator between the US and Iran.

“If the border dispute remains unresolved, Tehran may question whether Islamabad can simultaneously maintain productive relations with Iran and cooperate with Washington’s pressure campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Protests in France marred by rioting, looting: What to know
articles.summary: Protests in France descended into rioting and looting over the weekend as French President Emmanuel Macron called for calm. The protests started out in September at a high school in a suburb of Paris and were initially focused on teacher shortages and deteriorating building conditions. The protests then swiftly spread to other parts of the…
articles.body:
Protests in France descended into rioting and looting over the weekend as French President Emmanuel Macron called for calm.

The protests started out in September at a high school in a suburb of Paris and were initially focused on teacher shortages and deteriorating building conditions. The protests then swiftly spread to other parts of the country.

Since that time, fringe riots have engulfed the country, causing numerous clashes between the police and French protesters. The rioting reached a peak Saturday, which many politicians are now calling the worst social unrest France has seen in decades.

Macron said in a televised address to France that “those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”

The French president said he believed the riots were caused by “unrestrained violence” from “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has left the door open to declaring a state of emergency but has asked local leaders in several French cities to announce partial curfews, according to The Associated Press .

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said riots had broken out in Paris and across several other cities in France and that rioters had “looted and ransacked numerous businesses,” according to translation on social platform X .

“Attacking our law enforcement forces, targeting our institutions, degrading public buildings, breaking into prefectures or town halls, looting businesses: nothing can justify it,” Nuñez wrote. “From midday onward—in Marseille, from the morning—outrages were committed by several thousand far-left individuals determined to target our public buildings and confront our law enforcement forces.”

Nuñez confirmed that as of Sunday morning, more than 2,000 people had been taken into custody, while more than 600 law enforcement officers from various agencies had been injured.

“The material damage is considerable, particularly for several hundred business owners. The Republic will yield nothing to those who seek to impose disorder and violence,” he concluded on social media.

Nuñez has faced backlash from French politicians over the government’s response to the riots, resulting in him submitting his resignation over the weekend.

Macron rejected Nuñez’s resignation, telling him to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence,” according to France 24 .

French Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support for the thousands of businesses that had been damaged by riots, writing in a statement that “those ⁠who break ​things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” according to Reuters .

Disputes between French national and local government

The riots have divided French politicians as many feel Macron’s government did not respond sufficiently enough to the protests.

One city in France, Limoges, was ravaged by fires, and its 19th-century city hall is now largely destroyed.

Limoges Mayor Guillaume Guérin told Reuters that he believed there were not enough national police deployed to the city, adding that “there was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives.”

Far-right leader and French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen criticized Macron’s government directly on social media , saying it was “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness.”

Far-left leader and presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who backed the high school students’ movement, took part in the Paris protest Saturday. He has been critical of Nuñez, particularly, as he stated the Interior minister and “the police chiefs have shown complete incompetence.”

Mélenchon also called out law enforcement for using “dispersal grenades” on demonstrators, saying “people are being mutilated by the police.”

President Trump reiterated Monday that he believed the protests in France were caused by immigration to the country.

“The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST,” he wrote on Truth Social .

It’s unclear, however, how much any of the rioting had to do with immigration, as the protests were focused on better schooling facilities. The current demonstrations are backed by workers unions and appear to be mixing broader anger over the cost of living and rising prices in France.

images.caption: Police officers clash with high school students during a protest against education conditions that have disrupted classes across the country in Nancy, France on Oct. 5, 2026. Demonstrators pushed for expanded resources, improved school maintenance, smaller class sizes, and strategies to tackle staffing shortages. The countrywide action disrupted learning at roughly 400 to 500 high schools, which experienced full or partial class suspensions.

articles.title: How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?
articles.summary: Protesters across Europe have hit the streets amid anger over the cost of living.
articles.body:
Student protests in France are into their second month , escalating into demonstrations across Europe.

What began in September in France with pupils protesting against overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages has grown into wider anger at the cost of living and planned cuts to public services.

Protesters in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain have also taken to the streets over the lack of affordable housing, rising costs and failing public services – with many young people saying they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.

Facing their anger are leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron , Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez and Portugal’s PM Luis Montenegro. Sanchez belongs to the left, Meloni to the right and Macron and Montenegro are conservative-leaning centrists. But while their politics vary, they all face mounting unrest because of soaring costs of living.

Are they out of touch with the experiences and sentiments of youth in their countries? Al Jazeera visualises how prices, wages, housing and education have changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over the past 26 years, from when Macron, Meloni, Sanchez and Montenegro were in their 20s, much like many of the protesters angry with them.

How much more expensive is it compared to 2000?

The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.

Spain recorded the steepest increase at 78 percent, followed by Portugal at 71 percent, 68 percent in Italy and France at 59 percent.

That means goods and services that cost 100 euros ($112) in 2000 now cost about 178 euros ($200) in Spain, 171 euros ($192) in Portugal, 168 euros ($188) in Italy and 159 euros ($178) in France.

Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy, 8.3 percent in Spain, 8.1 percent in Portugal and 5.9 percent in France, the highest rate in all four countries since at least 2000.

The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By October that year, eight months into the war, energy prices across the eurozone were almost 42 percent higher than a year earlier, and food prices were also rising sharply, according to Eurostat .

Between 2021 and 2023, prices increased by 12 to 15 per cent in the four countries. Wages failed to keep up, and because prices do not fall back once inflation eases, many households are still feeling the squeeze today.

Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 per cent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 per cent in Spain, 11 per cent in France and 20 per cent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

In Spain most new jobs were in tourism and services, and were often seasonal and poorly paid, Jaime Velazquez, a journalist in Madrid, told Al Jazeera’s Inside Story .

Julius Fintelmann, cofounder and editor-in-chief of The European Correspondent, said ageing societies were squeezing out opportunities for younger workers, adding that the pay gap between older and younger workers has been widening across high-income economies for decades, so the promise that each generation would be better off than the last no longer holds.

Housing has become harder to afford in all four countries since 2000, according to the OECD’s price-to-income ratio. It provides a broad picture of how house prices have changed relative to incomes over time. When prices rise faster than incomes, the ratio goes up, suggesting homes are becoming less affordable on average.

However, it doesn’t show which households or regions are hit hardest, does not account for mortgage and borrowing costs, and says nothing about the quality of the homes people are paying for.

Spain has seen the biggest change. Its price-to-income ratio is 56 per cent higher than in 2000, even after falling sharply following the 2008 financial crisis.

In France, the ratio is 39 per cent higher than in 2000, though it has eased slightly since peaking in 2022.

Italy is the exception where house prices have broadly kept pace with incomes, leaving the ratio just 5 per cent higher than in 2000.

Portugal has seen the sharpest change in recent years. Its price-to-income ratio fell steadily for 15 years after 2000, meaning homes became more affordable. But since 2015 the ratio has risen by 67 per cent.

The OECD publishes the price-to-income ratio with 2015 as its reference year. To compare it with the wage and price data in this article, which started in 2000, Al Jazeera has reset the figures so that 2000 = 100.

How has state expenditure on education changed?

Education has been at the heart of the unrest in France, where protests began because of overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. While in Belgium and Albania, demonstrators have rallied against the rising cost of education and access to universities.

According to the latest data from Eurostat , France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.6 per cent in 2000.

Italy spent 4.4 per cent of its GDP on education compared to 4 per cent in 2024, Spain spent 4.1 per cent in 2000 and the same in 2024. Portugal spent 4.8 per cent in 2000 and 4.3 per cent in 2024.

articles.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
articles.summary: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to idenitify and remove listings linked to looting".
articles.body:
Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France .

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

French PM calls for partial curfews as he condemns 'thieves' and 'thugs' behind riots

Reuters news agency reported luxury shops and boutiques were shuttered and surrounded by security guards at the Place Vendome in Paris.

But it said a host of stores in the French capital, including Dior, Rolex, Louis Vuitton and Ralph Lauren had their shopfronts damaged

In Marseille, football club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted.

It has closed the store, along with fellow Ligue 1 club Lille, which said its club shop would remain closed until further notice.

articles.title: Kenyan cult leader found guilty over 190 children starved to death in the hope of ‘meeting Jesus’
articles.summary: The leader of a Kenyan Christian cult has been found guilty of the murder of 190 children through an organised system of enforced fasting and abuse.
articles.body: The leader of a Kenyan Christian cult has been found guilty of the murder of 190 children through an organised system of enforced fasting and abuse. Paul Mackenzie was on Monday convicted along with about 30 other suspects at Mombasa High Court over the deaths of 191 people, all but one of them children in Shakahola forest in eastern Kenya. Prosecutors have dubbed the trial one of Kenya’s “most consequential” criminal cases ever. The court found the deaths resulted from an “organised system in which religious teachings and an established hierarchy were used to direct and enforce deadly fasting among Mackenzie’s followers,” the office of the director of public prosecutions in Kenya said. “Fasting was implemented sequentially, beginning with children, while guards controlled movement and prevented followers from escaping,” the office said in a statement. Mackenzie also discouraged modern medicine and formal education, the court heard. Mackenzie, who is in his early 50s, and his co-accused were charged with the murders in 2024 after hundreds of children’s bodies were exhumed from Shakahola forest where Mackenzie and his associates were accused of running a death cult. Authorities started digging up bodies in Shakahola forest in April 2023. So far they have recovered 429 bodies. Further charges could follow. Mackenzie, who ran the Good News International Church, was accused of instructing his followers to starve themselves and their children to death so they could reach heaven and meet Jesus, CNN previously reported. Postmortem findings cited by Lady Justice Diana Kavedza on Monday indicated that some victims died from suffocation, neck compression or head injuries, rather than starvation alone. Mackenzie’s attorney Lawrence Obonyo told reporters Monday the defense team planned to appeal, saying his client maintained that he hadn’t forced anyone to fast and that the victims’ actions were voluntary. Search for justice In a lengthy ruling lasting more than eight hours on Monday, the judge described how Mackenzie used sermons and written materials to persuade followers that the outside world was evil, and that they could only find salvation by moving to the forest. Evidence extracted from his phone, including WhatsApp messages, showed communications with followers before they relocated to Shakahola, according to the judge. She said followers were persuaded to abandon their homes, families and livelihoods. The judge also described how those who resisted Mackenzie’s directive to fast were forced to comply. “Children were restrained, denied food and punished for attempting to eat or escape,” the director of public prosecutions said. CNN previously reported on families searching for relatives who had disappeared into Shakahola forest. Rodgers Shibutse, a Nairobi resident, said he found his mother’s remains among those exhumed in February 2024. Shibutse told CNN on Monday that Mackenzie had caused immense pain and that he wanted him sentenced to life in prison. Mackenzie and his co-accused will be handed their sentence on November 6. Asked whether that would bring justice for his mother, Shibutse said: “Not 100% justice, but at least the government has done something.”

images.caption: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie looks on during his court appearance at the Mombasa Law Court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday, October 19.

articles.title: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
articles.summary: It’s dark outside. The news cycle is relentless. But Finland’s national broadcaster has a solution: Adorable puppies, available any time, night or day.
articles.body: It’s dark outside. The news cycle is relentless. But Finland’s national broadcaster has a solution: Adorable puppies, available any time, night or day. Yle has been drawing millions of people to its website with “Pentulive” – Finnish for “Puppy Live” – a 24/7 live stream of Hilkka, a Lagotto Romagnolo dog, and her brand-new litter of puppies as they sleep, play and suckle enthusiastically. Hilkka gave birth to the two females and four males on October 10. The webcam was switched on shortly after, and the puppies will remain in the spotlight until they leave for their new homes in December. Given that puppies need up to 20 hours of sleep a day, the action can be limited, which may explain why “Pentulive,” now in its sixth season, has been labelled “slow TV” – a concept first trialed in Norway in 2009 with the Norwegian public broadcaster’s airing of a seven-hour train journey. Nonetheless, viewers who tune in to the home of the anonymous breeder have been promised the chance to witness some of the “puppies’ milestone moments,” according to a Yle press statement: from opening their eyes to learning to walk and having their first playtime outside. Despite Finland’s tiny population – just under 5.66 million – the “Pentulive” webpage had 6.5 million page views last year, according to Yle, and its social media channels attracted 20 million views. And based on viewing figures so far, this year’s puppies look set to outperform. One of the world’s northernmost countries, Finland is preparing to usher in its long, dark winter. Temperatures can drop as low as -50°C (-58°F) and in parts of the country north of the Arctic Circle the sun does not rise above the horizon for weeks on end. So it is hardly surprising that residents enjoy a cozy distraction from the bitter conditions outside. The puppy-cam was first launched in 2021 by Yle science reporter Pirjo Koskinen as part of a series on canine science. She told CNN in an email that the idea was, in part, “to shed light on a dog’s crucial first few weeks,” adding: “What happens at the breeder’s – much like with human children – influences the rest of the dog’s life.” Escape into the ‘puppy bubble’ Distraction from the harsh reality of daily life is part of “Pentulive“‘s appeal, Koskinen believes. “It is all about caring, love, and nurturing – all those positive aspects of humanity that often get pushed aside by a constant stream of unpleasant news,” she said. “‘Puppy Live’ offers comfort and relaxation amidst the rush of everyday life; it’s a wonderful escape from the human world into a ‘puppy bubble.’” Sonja Mutanen, a doctoral researcher studying media and animals at the University of Eastern Finland, explained its particular appeal to Finns. “For many viewers, these live streams are a much-anticipated highlight of the dark Finnish winter months,” she told CNN. “This kind of feel-good content can foster a sense of belonging and emotional well-being, which is important during late autumn and winter when people tend to stay at home more.” Live streams offer something different Miiamaaria Kujala, adjunct professor of comparative cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki, said in an email to CNN that a live feed affects us in a completely different way from the short reels that are now commonplace on social media. “The live stream offers something that appears to be missing from many of the modern busy lives: something real, genuine and fragile,” she said. “Pentulive is life-paced: It contains very calm periods and unexpectable action periods. As a live feed, it likely provokes more intense emotional responses from the observers … but it is also immensely calming to observe a sleeping puppy.” It also provides a “sense of continuity as it follows the puppies growing older,” she said, adding: “They’re not just random animals, you learn to know them individually.” This is the second litter for 5-year-old Hilkka, who is currently on leave from her role as a “school dog,” where she provides emotional support for pupils. So far, the fluffballs have only been given nicknames by their breeder, but on Saturday they will be officially renamed. The viewing public will narrow down a selection of names, from which the puppies themselves will “choose” – by sitting in a circle of sealed envelopes and snuffling at the one that appeals.

Viewers will be able to watch the newborn dogs 24/7 until they move to their new homes in December.
The litter is made up of two females and four males.

articles.title: Kenyan court convicts starvation cult leader of murdering 191 people
articles.summary: Doomsday sect leader Paul ⁠⁠Mackenzie had denied ordering the victims to starve so they could ‘meet Jesus’.
articles.body:
⁠A court in Kenya has found starvation cult leader Paul ⁠⁠Mackenzie and dozens of his associates guilty of murder over the deaths of 191 people – all but one of them children.

The self-proclaimed pastor and ⁠⁠his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death, so they could go to heaven before the world ended and “meet Jesus”.

Police arrested Mackenzie in 2023 after receiving a tip-off. After several weeks, authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.

Mackenzie, who was convicted along with 28 associates, insisted that he did not force the victims to starve, but that was dismissed by the court in Mombasa, where the verdict was announced on Monday.

The defendants had pleaded not guilty and denied charges in other cases, including terrorism, radicalisation, and stopping children from attaining an education.

The court said Mackenzie and others convicted in the case will be sentenced on November 6.

More than 400 people died in the Shakahola tragedy, according to Kenyan authorities, making it one of the country’s deadliest cult-related disasters.

Investigations uncovered mass graves and evidence of severe malnutrition, triggering nationwide scrutiny of religious extremism and the government’s failure to detect the group’s activities earlier.

Since the bodies were discovered three years ago, there have been calls for the government to impose tougher regulations on religious organisations. It also emerged that Mackenzie was arrested twice in the past but then released.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie had “initiated and directed” extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325-hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest.

They described a “structured hierarchy of death” under which children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.

Family members of the victims who died in the forest came to hear the verdict at the Mombasa court.

Francis Wanje lost eight family members, including two grandchildren, to the cult.

“It has been really a heavy thing (for) us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems,” the 62-year-old said.
